title: Chapter 87 – The Cost of Two Pills
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The market town of Qingshi holds its auction in a warehouse by the river, and by the second bell the room is so full that the lamps burn blue for want of air.

Jian stands at the back with his hood up and a pangolin asleep in his sleeve. He has come in the company of Tan Ruyan, who walks ahead of him through the crowd in a silver-gray cloak with a bodyguard on either side, and who has told the doorkeeper that the small boy at her heel is a cousin on the mother's side. The doorkeeper has looked at the boy, and at the cloak, and at the Tan family seal on the pass, and waved them through.

"Lot nineteen," says Tan Ruyan, without turning her head. "After the iron-bark and before the snow-lotus. If the bidding follows form, it will start at eighty stones and close near three hundred."

"I have eleven."

"I know what you have." She does not smile. "That is why you are standing behind me."

The hall is a long barn of a room, rafters hung with paper lanterns, benches filled with merchants in furs and silks. At the far end, on a low platform, an auctioneer in a green robe stands behind a lacquered table with a gavel in his hand. Behind him, on a row of stands, lie the lots: bundles of herbs in cloth, jars of tinctures, a coil of rope that glimmers like silver, a small black box with a lock.

Lot eighteen sells for sixty stones. Lot nineteen is brought out by a clerk on a silk cushion.

It is a pouch of pale gray leather, no larger than his fist. The auctioneer opens it, tilts it to the lamplight, and a fine glittering powder falls in a thread across the cushion. It is white as milk and bright as frost. It catches the light and breaks it into small cold stars.

"Pale jade powder," says the auctioneer. "One liang. Level 2, ground from a sixth-year spirit jade by the late Master Wu of Cloud Peak. Sealed in leather, unopened, tested to quality medium." He sets down the pouch. "Starting at eighty."

A hush. Then a dozen hands.

Jian watches Tan Ruyan lift one finger.

* * *

The bidding is quick and bruising.

It begins at eighty and leaps to a hundred and fifty in the first breath. A heavy man in sable raises it to two hundred. A woman in violet raises it to two-fifty. Tan Ruyan lifts her finger every time, calmly, without hurry, as a person might lift a cup. The numbers go up and the hall grows quiet. By three hundred there are only three bidders. By three-twenty there are two.

"Three-forty," says the man in sable.

"Three-fifty," says Tan Ruyan.

"Three-seventy."

She does not look at the man. She looks at the pouch on its cushion, and then, briefly, over her shoulder, at Jian. In her eyes there is a question. He gives her a very small nod.

"Four hundred," she says.

The man in sable draws a breath. He glares at the auctioneer, at the girl, at the crowd. A bead of sweat slides down his temple. Then he lowers his hand and sits back, and the gavel falls with a crack.

"Sold. Four hundred stones, to the Tan family of Qingshi."

The hall breaks into noise. Tan Ruyan does not move. She waits until the clerk has carried the pouch to the cashier's cage, and then she says, still not turning, in a voice so low that he has to lean to catch it:

"Four hundred. You understand that I have just paid more than the powder is worth."

"Yes."

"I did it because I said I would. I said I would bid under the Tan name." Her mouth thins. "My father will ask what I wanted it for. I will say it was for my own pill."

"It was for mine."

"It was for ours." She turns, at last. "Where is the root?"

He takes it out. It is wrapped in dry moss inside a box of cold jade, the second Earthheart root, the one the Overseer allowed him, the one he has carried against his ribs for twelve days. He holds it out, and the lamps catch the dull russet of the skin and the faint red fibers. Tan Ruyan's pupils widen.

"I said what you could trade me for it," she says, softly.

"I said I would think."

"And?"

"It is Level 2. It is worth more than the powder." He sets it in her palm. "I would rather you had it than anyone."

Her fingers close on the box.

For a moment she does not speak. She stands among the roaring merchants, in her silver-gray cloak, with her face half in lamplight, and he sees something in it that is not calculation and not pride. It is an expression he has seen on Feng's face, on the stair.

"You are a very strange person," she says.

"I have been told."

"I will pay the difference." She slides the pouch of jade powder into his hands, under the cover of her cloak. "Not in stones. In favors. I keep a ledger too, you know." A short, bright, crooked smile. "I will let you know when I want it called."

She is gone into the crowd before he can answer.

* * *

The Medicine Valley market is a street of stalls along the river, and on the afternoon of the sixteenth, there is a new one.

It stands at the lower end, under a red awning, between a seller of dried fish and a woman with baskets of persimmons. A small table, a straw mat, a few sacks of herbs. Nothing remarkable. A woman in a plain brown wool robe sits behind it with her hands in her lap, a straw hat shading her face. A few passing disciples stop, ask the price of bitterwort, and move on.

Jian stops.

He does not say anything. He stands in the thin snow in front of the table with his hands in his sleeves and his mouth shut. The woman does not look up. She is sorting a handful of dry roots by length, laying them out on the mat in a row. Her fingers are quick and gentle and a little chapped.

"Bitterwort is two stones the bundle," she says. "Marsh-lily is three. The Heartroot is not for sale."

"Who is it for?"

"A boy." She sets down the last root. "Who has been very busy."

He does not trust himself to speak.

The straw hat lifts. Gray eyes look up at him, steady and clear and a little bright. There are new lines at the corners of them. There is a streak of white in the hair at her temple, and she is thinner than she was in the Garden, and she is smiling, very slightly, in the way she smiles when she has been waiting a long time and does not intend to make a fuss.

"I came to sell roots," says Su Qinghe.

"Mother."

"I am a herb-factor for the Pill Hall. I have a license. I have a stall. I will be here every afternoon, in all weathers, until the end of the season." She folds her hands. "I will not ask what you have done. I will not ask what you are doing. I will sit here and sort roots, and if you want to talk, you will come and buy a bundle of bitterwort. It is two stones."

He lays two stones on the table.

It is all he has. It is, he sees, a thing she knew he would do.

"Sit," she says. She indicates a low stool. "Take a bundle. Take two. The Heartroot is yours. I brought it from home, nine years old. Garden-grown, dried in the shade." She pushes a small cloth bundle across the mat. "I was told you would need it for a pill."

"Who told you?"

"Bai wrote to your father." A faint dry smile. "I read it over his shoulder."

He sits. He takes the bundle. It is light and warm and smells of rain and earth, the smell of a kitchen in the Garden, the smell of the first spring. A knot rises in his throat. He swallows it. For a time neither of them speaks. The river runs under the bridge. A child laughs in the street. An old man with a basket of persimmons calls the price of his wares in a cracked sing-song.

"You have grown," she says.

"A little."

"Not in height." She lays a hand over his, on the table. It is dry and warm. "I will ask you only one thing."

He waits.

"Are you eating?"

A laugh breaks out of him, surprised and cracked. He puts his free hand over his face.

"Yes, Mother."

"Good." Her fingers tighten. "Then we can begin."

* * *

The writs come on the twentieth day after the Elders' notice, in a single envelope, with a plum-colored seal.

Bai hands it over in the furnace room without ceremony. He is sitting beside the bronze with his feet up on the stone ring and a paper twist of plums in his lap, looking more rumpled than usual, and a little gray under the eyes. "Two," he says. "Dew from the Treasury, cinnabar from Furnace Peak. Both signed. Both sealed. The Treasury keeper wanted to know why a Pill Hall apprentice needed three drops of Azure dew. I told him it was none of his business. He said it was exactly his business." He eats a plum. "I paid for it."

"Elder, the price. My father wrote—"

"Your father wrote a very civil letter." The pale eyes crease. "I received it this morning. I read it twice and put it in a drawer. I do not often read a letter twice." He swallows. "A night in the Garden. I shall remember that."

"May I ask what you mean to do with it?"

"No." Bai's face is perfectly mild. "I would not know what to say. But I will tell you this. It has to do with a pill, and a boy, and a thing I should have done fifty-two years ago." He brushes crumbs from his robe. "Go and fetch your reagents. I will have the Treasury's man wait outside."

The Treasury's man is a thin, stooped, officious clerk with a leather satchel and a bronze key on a chain. He stands in the passage with his chin raised. When Jian comes out, he looks him up and down and hands over a glass vial the size of a thumb, stoppered with wax. Inside, three drops of liquid turn slowly in the lamplight. It is clear as water. It has a faint blue tinge. It smells of ice.

"Azure dew," says the clerk. "Signed for. Do not drop it."

From Furnace Peak, the next afternoon, a young woman with soot on her cheeks brings a lacquer box. Inside, on a bed of ash, lie two grains of red crystal no larger than rice, so bright that they seem to burn through the wood. The box is warm. The grains hum.

"Sun-forged cinnabar," says the woman. "Sign here."

He signs.

Wei Chen brings the last thing himself, on the evening of the twenty-second day. He appears at the Pill Hall gate in his indigo cloak, with his long calm face grave, and in his hands a clay pot wrapped in sacking. He sets it on the step.

"The Overseer asks me to say," he says, "that he has been persuaded. It is the tenth stem. The Valley's mother vine." He pauses. "It will not regrow for three years. He wept when he cut it. I would be obliged if you did not mention that."

"I will not."

"He said to tell you that the beasts are coming back." Wei Chen inclines his head. "He said that was payment enough."

Jian lifts the sacking. In the pot, in black earth, coils a single thick stem, nine feet long, knotted nine times, green as new jade. A pale sap beads on the cut. It smells like marrow.

Ninefold marrow vine. Level 2.

He looks at it for a long time.

All of it, he thinks. Every reagent. In forty-seven days.

It is not a thing he can believe.

* * *

He makes the first pill at midnight, in a locked room, with his back to the door.

It is the Pill Hall's store of spare vessels, a narrow stone cell behind the herb store with a table, a stool, a lamp, and a brass-bound chest of unused jars. Bai has given him the key. "You will not be disturbed," he said, with his eyes on the ceiling. "I am going out to look at the stars. I shall stand a hundred paces off, with my back to this building, and I shall not turn my head."

He lays out the reagents on the table, in a row.

Earthheart root. Azure dew, three drops. Second-rank marrow, one vial. Pale jade powder, one liang. Sun-forged cinnabar, two grains. They look like very little. A root, a bottle, a pouch, a vial, a box. He puts his right hand on the table beside them, palm down, and the panel opens.

```
SYNTHESIS — Foundation Establishment Pill (Level 2)
Formula: recorded (scan, ch73).
Reagents: 5/5 present. Quality check:
Earthheart root ... OK (mature, whole)
Azure dew ... OK (3 drops, sealed)
Second-rank beast marrow ... OK (fresh, cold-stored)
Pale jade powder ... OK (1 liang, medium)
Sun-forged cinnabar ... OK (2 grains, unflawed)
Fire sequence: 9 stages, one night, steady middle. Provided by Interface.
Resonance step: provided by Interface (cradle-assisted).
Cost: 150 CE.
CE: 180 -> 30.
Reagents will be consumed. Output: 1 pill.
Predicted quality: top.

PROCEED? [Y / N]
```

He reads it slowly.

One pill. One chance. There is no second try. If the Interface fails, if the formula is flawed, if the resonance step falters, the reagents are gone and the energy with them. The Founder's own pill sits in a locked box in Bai's furnace room, and it is the only other one in the world.

He thinks of Feng, lying on a cot with his leg in splints. Of Tan Ruyan, who paid four hundred stones for a bag of dust. Of Heng, in the cold cell, who lies awake and reads. Of a boy of nine or ten, six hundred years ago, who climbed the stair and did not come down, and for whom a pill was made, and never taken.

I am taking it.

Y.

The room goes white.

* * *

It takes the whole night, and he is awake for all of it.

He sits on the stool with his hand flat on the table and watches. The reagents do not burn. They do not boil. They rise from the wood in slow gleaming threads, one after another, and wind into the air above the table: the red of the cinnabar, the pale gold of the marrow, the white of the jade, the blue of the dew, the russet of the root. They braid. They turn. They form a column of light as tall as his arm and as thin as a reed, spinning slowly in the lamp's glow, and from it comes a note.

It is the same note he heard in the Founder's pill. It is lower. It is richer. It is a sound like a very large bell heard from a very great distance, and it goes through the stone cell and the stone floor and the mountain.

At the third hour the column bends. At the fifth, it folds in on itself, ring on ring, until it is a sphere. At the seventh, the sphere begins to shrink. It shrinks as a drop of ink shrinks on a hot plate, drawing in, drawing in, until it is a single bright point no bigger than a pea.

At the ninth hour, it falls.

It drops on the table with a tiny sound, like a bead on a drum. It lies on the wood, round, pale gold, a little smaller than a hazelnut. A faint slow pulse moves through it. Once every few breaths, it breathes.

He picks it up.

It is warm. It hums against his palm, and in the center of his chest, below the breastbone, something answers: the Seal, slow and deep, a single low note held for the length of a breath. It has recognized the pill. It has recognized the thing the pill was made for.

```
SYNTHESIS COMPLETE.
Item: Foundation Establishment Pill (Level 2).
Quality: top.
CE: 30.
```

He lays it on a square of white silk. He folds the silk over it. His hands, he sees, are shaking, and his tunic is soaked to the skin.

Thirty.

He has thirty points of energy left in a mind that feels, for the first time in a year, quite empty. The panel, quiet, has dimmed to a faint steady glow. Beyond the door, in the cold dark, an old man stands a hundred paces off with his back to the building and his head tilted to the stars.

It is a long time before Jian can make himself stand.

* * *

The second pill he must make with his hands.

Bai has said it plainly. "The Nine Turn is a Level 1 pill, peak tier. It is taught to no one, because it cannot be taught; the fire has to be felt. I have made it four times in ninety years, and I have failed it twice. You have a Rank 1 license and a fire root. If you can do it, you can do it. If you cannot, you cannot, and you will lose the lotus." He eats a plum. "I will not lie to you about the cost."

"How much?"

"The lotus. The vine. The Heartroot. Your mother's nine-year-old Heartroot, which is the best I have seen in thirty years." The pale eyes rest on him. "And my furnace. For the whole of a night. I do not lend it. I will not lend it to you. I will charge a fee."

"What fee, Elder?"

"One pill."

"One of the two?"

"If the batch makes two, I take one. If it makes one, I take half." A shrug. "It is the standard rate. The furnace is the Founders' bronze. It has not been lit for the Nine Turn in nineteen years. It will burn the lotus if you let it." He lifts a finger. "If you do not let it, it will burn the vine instead."

Jian stands in the furnace room at dusk with the five reagents laid out on the stone ring, and the great bronze mouth glowing dully in front of him. He has Frostbell and Mourner's cup from the store, the Heartroot from his mother, the vine in its pot, the lotus in its jade box. He has Pebble on his shoulder and a gray line of cold sweat down his spine.

A Rank 1 craft limit. A peak-tier pill. The top of what I can do.

He sits down cross-legged before the furnace.

He does not use the panel. It would not help. This is not Synthesis; this is a boy and a fire, and the thirty points of energy he has left are not for this. He looks into the bronze mouth and lets his eyes soften and the heat open.

Warm. Warmer. There.

He feeds the vine first.

It goes in as a coil, nine knots, green as jade, and the flame takes it with a hiss like a drawn breath. He watches the color change. He watches the edges brown. He counts nothing. He feels the heat in the soles of his feet and the base of his skull, and when the moment comes, a shade before the vine begins to char, he lifts it out with the bone tongs and lays it in a dish.

One.

The Heartroot is next. Then the Frostbell, seven pinches, one by one. Then the Mourner's cup, nine petals, each placed in the flame at the exact instant the previous petal has gone transparent. He does not hurry. He does not slow. The fire is a living thing and he is a part of it, and for hour after hour, as the night wears on and the bronze ticks and the lamp burns low, there is nothing in the world but heat.

At the fifth hour, the lotus.

It is the last thing. It goes in last, because it is the most delicate, and he holds it above the flame in the tongs. The gray bud trembles. The petals curl. A thin pale smoke rises from them, and the smell of rain on cold stone fills the room.

Now.

He hesitates.

It is a hair's breadth. A flicker of doubt, no more. The flame beneath him gutters, a little, in its bed of coals, and the heat dips, and he sees the lotus petals begin to blacken at the tips.

No.

Pebble's claws dig into his collar. Hot. Too hot. Back.

He yanks the tongs. The bud swings free of the flame with the edge of one petal curled and burnt, and he lays it in the dish and stares at it with his heart going like a drum.

I nearly lost it.

It is a long moment before he can steady his hands. The lotus is whole. One petal is charred to a thread. It will have to do.

He puts it in.

* * *

Dawn comes gray through the vent.

He sits on the stone, with his hands in his lap and his back against the ring, too tired to think. The furnace has cooled to a dull red. Bai sits on his low stool across the bronze, eating nothing, watching him. He has been sitting there for hours. He has not said a word.

Jian lifts the lid.

Two pills lie at the bottom of the kettle.

They are small and round, the size of a pea, and they are the color of old pewter. They do not shine. They do not hum. They lie in the ash with the quiet, dense, patient weight of lead. Beside him, the Elder lets out a long slow breath.

"Two," says Bai.

"Two."

"Quality?"

Jian picks one up. It is heavy. It is cool. A faint slow pull runs through his arm, like a hand taking his pulse. He turns it over and sees, on the gray surface, nine very small concentric rings, so fine that they might have been drawn with a hair.

"Medium," he says. "Not top. One of the petals burned."

"Medium." The old man rubs his face. "Level 1, peak tier, quality medium. Hand-brewed by an apprentice in his second month." His voice is odd. "I have been alchemist to this Sect for ninety years, boy, and I have never seen a Nine Turn at medium on a first attempt. I have seen it burn. I have seen it crack. I have seen it come out as a lump of ash and a ruined lotus. I did not think I would see it done."

"I nearly lost it."

"Everyone nearly loses it." Bai holds out his palm. "That is the fee."

Jian places the second pill in it.

The Elder closes his fingers. He sits for a moment with his eyes shut, a stout, rumpled man in a stained robe, with a gray pill in his fist and an expression of unutterable tiredness. Then he opens his eyes and says, quite gently:

"Go and sleep. You have three days."

"Three days?"

"The Stillness Chambers are booked." He tucks the pill into his sleeve. "I took the liberty. Chamber nine, the deep one, under the Library. Three days of silence. It is the only room in the Court where a Foundation breakthrough will not be felt on the stair." The pale eyes crease. "I am told the Elders are watching the landing. I did not want them to watch you."

Jian stares at him.

"Elder."

"Do not thank me." Bai turns toward the door. "I am a man who does not like to sign things."

In the cold light of the vent, Jian wraps the two pills in white silk and lays them in a box of jade: the gold one, warm and breathing, the gray one, heavy and still. He closes the lid. The panel, dim at the edge of his sight, brightens by a hair, and a single small line lights in the corner.

```
Foundation window: opens in 3 days.
Anchor (landing 40): AWAKENING.
```
